raw: CHAPTER VI. Hundreds of People
en: [Chapter 6] Hundreds of People

raw: The quiet lodgings of Doctor Manette were in a quiet street-corner not far from Soho-square.
en: The quiet lodgings of Doctor Manette were in a quiet street corner not far from Soho Square.

raw: On the afternoon of a certain fine Sunday when the waves of four months had rolled over the trial for treason, and carried it, as to the public interest and memory, far out to sea, Mr.
en: On a fine Sunday afternoon, four months after the treason trial had passed and been mostly forgotten by the public, Mr.

raw: Jarvis Lorry walked along the sunny streets from Clerkenwell where he lived, on his way to dine with the Doctor.
en: Jarvis Lorry walked from his home in Clerkenwell to have dinner with the Doctor.

raw: After several relapses into business-absorption, Mr.
en: After initially focusing only on business, Mr.

raw: Lorry had become the Doctor’s friend, and the quiet street-corner was the sunny part of his life.
en: Lorry had become a true friend of the family, and this quiet street corner had become the happiest part of his life.

raw: On this certain fine Sunday, Mr.
en: On this pleasant Sunday, Mr.

raw: Lorry walked towards Soho, early in the afternoon, for three reasons of habit.
en: Lorry walked toward Soho early in the afternoon for three habitual reasons.

raw: Firstly, because, on fine Sundays, he often walked out, before dinner, with the Doctor and Lucie; secondly, because, on unfavourable Sundays, he was accustomed to be with them as the family friend, talking, reading, looking out of window, and generally getting through the day; thirdly, because he happened to have his own little shrewd doubts to solve, and knew how the ways of the Doctor’s household pointed to that time as a likely time for solving them.
en: First, because on nice Sundays he often walked before dinner with the Doctor and Lucie. Second, because on bad Sundays he spent the day with them as a family friend. They would talk, read, look out the window, and simply pass the time together. Third, because he had some small doubts he wanted to resolve, and he knew this was a good time to observe the Doctor's household.

raw: A quainter corner than the corner where the Doctor lived, was not to be found in London.
en: A more charming corner than the one where the Doctor lived could not be found in London.

raw: There was no way through it, and the front windows of the Doctor’s lodgings commanded a pleasant little vista of street that had a congenial air of retirement on it.
en: It was a dead-end street, and the front windows of the lodgings looked out onto a pleasant, quiet street.

raw: There were few buildings then, north of the Oxford-road, and forest-trees flourished, and wild flowers grew, and the hawthorn blossomed, in the now vanished fields.
en: There were few buildings north of Oxford Road back then, and forest trees and wild flowers still grew in fields that have now vanished.

raw: As a consequence, country airs circulated in Soho with vigorous freedom, instead of languishing into the parish like stray paupers without a settlement; and there was many a good south wall, not far off, on which the peaches ripened in their season.
en: As a result, fresh country air circulated freely in Soho, and nearby walls were lined with peaches ripening in the sun.

raw: The summer light struck into the corner brilliantly in the earlier part of the day; but, when the streets grew hot, the corner was in shadow, though not in shadow so remote but that you could see beyond it into a glare of brightness.
en: The summer sun shone brightly into the corner early in the day; but when the streets grew hot, the corner was in the shade.

raw: It was a cool spot, staid but cheerful, a wonderful place for echoes, and a very harbour from the raging streets.
en: It was a cool, peaceful but cheerful spot, famous for its echoes, and a quiet refuge from the busy streets.

raw: There ought to have been a tranquil bark in such an anchorage, and there was.
en: The Doctor rented two floors of a large, quiet house.

raw: The Doctor occupied two floors of a large stiff house, where several callings purported to be pursued by day, but whereof little was audible any day, and which was shunned by all of them at night.
en: A few businesses operated there during the day, but they made very little noise and were empty at night.

raw: In a building at the back, attainable by a courtyard where a plane-tree rustled its green leaves, church-organs claimed to be made, and silver to be chased, and likewise gold to be beaten by some mysterious giant who had a golden arm starting out of the wall of the front hall--as if he had beaten himself precious, and menaced a similar conversion of all visitors.
en: In a building at the back, reached through a courtyard with a green plane tree, organs were made, silver was engraved, and gold was beaten. The craftsman who did this had hung a sign of a golden arm extending from the front hall wall. It looked as if he had turned his own arm to gold and was threatening to do the same to visitors.

raw: Very little of these trades, or of a lonely lodger rumoured to live up-stairs, or of a dim coach-trimming maker asserted to have a counting-house below, was ever heard or seen.
en: Very little was ever seen or heard of these trades, or of a quiet lodger upstairs, or of a coachmaker downstairs.

raw: Occasionally, a stray workman putting his coat on, traversed the hall, or a stranger peered about there, or a distant clink was heard across the courtyard, or a thump from the golden giant.
en: Occasionally a workman walked through the hall, a stranger looked around, or a distant clinking sound was heard from the courtyard.

raw: These, however, were only the exceptions required to prove the rule that the sparrows in the plane-tree behind the house, and the echoes in the corner before it, had their own way from Sunday morning unto Saturday night.
en: Aside from these rare noises, the sparrows in the tree and the echoes in the street had the place to themselves all week.

raw: Doctor Manette received such patients here as his old reputation, and its revival in the floating whispers of his story, brought him.
en: Doctor Manette saw patients here, drawn by his old reputation and the rumors of his dramatic story.

raw: His scientific knowledge, and his vigilance and skill in conducting ingenious experiments, brought him otherwise into moderate request, and he earned as much as he wanted.
en: His scientific knowledge and skill in conducting experiments also kept him in demand, earning him as much money as he needed.

raw: These things were within Mr.
en: Mr.

raw: Jarvis Lorry’s knowledge, thoughts, and notice, when he rang the door-bell of the tranquil house in the corner, on the fine Sunday afternoon.
en: Lorry was thinking of these things when he rang the doorbell on that fine Sunday afternoon.

raw: “Doctor Manette at home?”
en: "Is Doctor Manette at home?"

raw: Expected home.
en: He was expected back soon.

raw: “Miss Lucie at home?”
en: "Is Miss Lucie at home?"

raw: Expected home.
en: She was also expected back soon.

raw: “Miss Pross at home?”
en: "Is Miss Pross at home?"

raw: Possibly at home, but of a certainty impossible for handmaid to anticipate intentions of Miss Pross, as to admission or denial of the fact.
en: She might be, but it was impossible for the servant girl to guess whether Miss Pross wanted to see visitors or not.

raw: “As I am at home myself,” said Mr.
en: "Since I feel at home here myself," said Mr.

raw: Lorry, “I’ll go upstairs.”
en: Lorry, "I’ll go upstairs."

raw: Although the Doctor’s daughter had known nothing of the country of her birth, she appeared to have innately derived from it that ability to make much of little means, which is one of its most useful and most agreeable characteristics.
en: Although Lucie had no memory of France, the country of her birth, she seemed to have inherited the French ability to make a place look beautiful with very little money.

raw: Simple as the furniture was, it was set off by so many little adornments, of no value but for their taste and fancy, that its effect was delightful.
en: Simple as the furniture was, it was decorated with so many tasteful little ornaments that the effect was delightful.

raw: The disposition of everything in the rooms, from the largest object to the least; the arrangement of colours, the elegant variety and contrast obtained by thrift in trifles, by delicate hands, clear eyes, and good sense; were at once so pleasant in themselves, and so expressive of their originator, that, as Mr.
en: The way everything in the rooms was set up, from the largest object to the smallest, was incredibly pleasant. The colors, the elegant variety, and the beautiful contrasts created by careful choices and a delicate touch were all so expressive of the person who designed them, that as Mr.

raw: Lorry stood looking about him, the very chairs and tables seemed to ask him, with something of that peculiar expression which he knew so well by this time, whether he approved?
en: Lorry stood looking around, even the chairs and tables seemed to ask him with that familiar expression whether he approved of it all.

raw: There were three rooms on a floor, and, the doors by which they communicated being put open that the air might pass freely through them all, Mr.
en: There were three rooms on the floor, and the doors between them were kept open to let the breeze pass through.

raw: Lorry, smilingly observant of that fanciful resemblance which he detected all around him, walked from one to another.
en: Mr. Lorry walked from one room to another, smiling at the pleasant atmosphere.

raw: The first was the best room, and in it were Lucie’s birds, and flowers, and books, and desk, and work-table, and box of water-colours; the second was the Doctor’s consulting-room, used also as the dining-room; the third, changingly speckled by the rustle of the plane-tree in the yard, was the Doctor’s bedroom, and there, in a corner, stood the disused shoemaker’s bench and tray of tools, much as it had stood on the fifth floor of the dismal house by the wine-shop, in the suburb of Saint Antoine in Paris.
en: The first was the best room. It contained Lucie's birds, flowers, books, desk, and watercolors. The second was the Doctor’s consulting room, which was also used for dining. The third, shaded by the leaves of the plane tree outside, was the Doctor’s bedroom. In the corner stood the unused shoemaker’s bench and tools, looking just as they had in the dark attic room in Paris.

raw: “I wonder,” said Mr.
en: "I wonder," said Mr.

raw: Lorry, pausing in his looking about, “that he keeps that reminder of his sufferings about him!”
en: Lorry, looking around, "why he keeps that painful reminder of his suffering!"

raw: “And why wonder at that?” was the abrupt inquiry that made him start.
en: "And why shouldn't he?" came a sharp voice that made him jump.

raw: It proceeded from Miss Pross, the wild red woman, strong of hand, whose acquaintance he had first made at the Royal George Hotel at Dover, and had since improved.
en: It was Miss Pross, the eccentric, red-haired woman whom Mr. Lorry had first met at the Dover hotel and had since come to know well.

raw: “I should have thought--” Mr.
en: "I would have thought, " Mr.

raw: Lorry began.
en: Lorry began.

raw: “Pooh!
en: "Bah!

raw: You’d have thought!” said Miss Pross; and Mr. Lorry left off.
en: What you would have thought!" said Miss Pross, cutting him off.

raw: “How do you do?” inquired that lady then--sharply, and yet as if to express that she bore him no malice.
en: "How do you do?" she asked sharply, though not unkindly.

raw: “I am pretty well, I thank you,” answered Mr.
en: "I am well, thank you," answered Mr.

raw: Lorry, with meekness; “how are you?”
en: Lorry meekly. "How are you?"

raw: “Nothing to boast of,” said Miss Pross.
en: "Nothing to brag about," said Miss Pross.

raw: “Indeed?”
en: "Indeed?"

raw: “Ah! indeed!” said Miss Pross. “I am very much put out about my Ladybird.”
en: "Yes, indeed!" said Miss Pross. "I am very annoyed about my Ladybird."

raw: “Indeed?”
en: "Indeed?"

raw: “For gracious sake say something else besides ‘indeed,’ or you’ll fidget me to death,” said Miss Pross: whose character (dissociated from stature) was shortness.
en: "For heaven's sake, say something other than 'indeed,' or you will drive me crazy," said Miss Pross. She was known for her bluntness.

raw: “Really, then?” said Mr.
en: "Really, then?" Mr.

raw: Lorry, as an amendment.
en: Lorry corrected himself.

raw: “Really, is bad enough,” returned Miss Pross, “but better.
en: Miss Pross returned, "Really is bad enough, but better.

raw: Yes, I am very much put out.”
en: Yes, I am very upset."

raw: “May I ask the cause?”
en: "May I ask why?"

raw: “I don’t want dozens of people who are not at all worthy of Ladybird, to come here looking after her,” said Miss Pross.
en: "I don't want dozens of people who are not good enough for Ladybird coming here to see her," said Miss Pross.

raw: “_Do_ dozens come for that purpose?”
en: "Do dozens of people actually come for that?"

raw: “Hundreds,” said Miss Pross.
en: "Hundreds," said Miss Pross.

raw: It was characteristic of this lady (as of some other people before her time and since) that whenever her original proposition was questioned, she exaggerated it.
en: It was typical of Miss Pross to exaggerate whenever anyone questioned her statements.

raw: “Dear me!” said Mr.
en: "Dear me!" said Mr.

raw: Lorry, as the safest remark he could think of.
en: Lorry, choosing the safest response.

raw: “I have lived with the darling--or the darling has lived with me, and paid me for it; which she certainly should never have done, you may take your affidavit, if I could have afforded to keep either myself or her for nothing--since she was ten years old.
en: "I have lived with the darling—or rather, the darling has lived with me and paid me for it. You can be sure she would never have had to pay a cent if I could have afforded to support us both for free—ever since she was ten years old.

raw: And it’s really very hard,”  said Miss Pross.
en: "And it’s very hard now."

raw: Not seeing with precision what was very hard, Mr.
en: Not understanding what was so hard, Mr.

raw: Lorry shook his head; using that important part of himself as a sort of fairy cloak that would fit anything.
en: Lorry shook his head, using it as a kind of magic cloak that could mean almost anything.

raw: “All sorts of people who are not in the least degree worthy of the pet, are always turning up,” said Miss Pross. “When you began it--”
en: "All sorts of unworthy people are always showing up," said Miss Pross. "Ever since you started it."

raw: “_I_ began it, Miss Pross?”
en: "_I_ started it, Miss Pross?"

raw: “Didn’t you?
en: "Didn't you?

raw: Who brought her father to life?”
en: Who brought her father back to life?"

raw: “Oh!
en: "Oh!

raw: If _that_ was beginning it--” said Mr.
en: If _that_ was starting it, " said Mr.

raw: Lorry.
en: Lorry.

raw: “It wasn’t ending it, I suppose?
en: "It wasn't ending it, was it?

raw: I say, when you began it, it was hard enough; not that I have any fault to find with Doctor Manette, except that he is not worthy of such a daughter, which is no imputation on him, for it was not to be expected that anybody should be, under any circumstances.
en: When you started it, it was hard enough. I have no complaint about Doctor Manette, except that he is not worthy of such a daughter, though no one could be.

raw: But it really is doubly and trebly hard to have crowds and multitudes of people turning up after him (I could have forgiven him), to take Ladybird’s affections away from me.”
en: But it is doubly hard to have crowds of people showing up after her to take her affection away from me."

raw: Mr.
en: Mr.

raw: Lorry knew Miss Pross to be very jealous, but he also knew her by this time to be, beneath the service of her eccentricity, one of those unselfish creatures--found only among women--who will, for pure love and admiration, bind themselves willing slaves, to youth when they have lost it, to beauty that they never had, to accomplishments that they were never fortunate enough to gain, to bright hopes that never shone upon their own sombre lives.
en: Lorry knew Miss Pross was very jealous, but he also knew that beneath her eccentric behavior, she was completely devoted to Lucie. She was one of those unselfish women who gladly dedicate their lives to serving the youth, beauty, and success they never had themselves.

raw: He knew enough of the world to know that there is nothing in it better than the faithful service of the heart; so rendered and so free from any mercenary taint, he had such an exalted respect for it, that in the retributive arrangements made by his own mind--we all make such arrangements, more or less--he stationed Miss Pross much nearer to the lower Angels than many ladies immeasurably better got up both by Nature and Art, who had balances at Tellson’s.
en: He knew enough about the world to realize there is nothing better than loyal, heartfelt service given without any greed. He had such deep respect for it that, in his own mind, he placed Miss Pross much closer to the angels than many naturally beautiful or dressed-up ladies who kept large bank accounts at Tellson's.

raw: “There never was, nor will be, but one man worthy of Ladybird,” said Miss Pross; “and that was my brother Solomon, if he hadn’t made a mistake in life.”
en: "There never was, and never will be, but one man worthy of Ladybird," said Miss Pross. "And that was my brother Solomon, if he hadn't made a mistake in life."

raw: Here again: Mr.
en: Mr.

raw: Lorry’s inquiries into Miss Pross’s personal history had established the fact that her brother Solomon was a heartless scoundrel who had stripped her of everything she possessed, as a stake to speculate with, and had abandoned her in her poverty for evermore, with no touch of compunction.
en: Lorry’s past inquiries had revealed that Solomon was actually a heartless thief who had stolen everything Miss Pross owned and abandoned her in poverty.

raw: Miss Pross’s fidelity of belief in Solomon (deducting a mere trifle for this slight mistake) was quite a serious matter with Mr.
en: Yet Miss Pross's blind faith in her brother, excusing his behavior as a "slight mistake", only increased Mr.

raw: Lorry, and had its weight in his good opinion of her.
en: Lorry, and it certainly helped shape his good opinion of her.

raw: “As we happen to be alone for the moment, and are both people of business,” he said, when they had got back to the drawing-room and had sat down there in friendly relations, “let me ask you--does the Doctor, in talking with Lucie, never refer to the shoemaking time, yet?”
en: As they sat down in the living room he said, "Since we are alone and are both practical people, let me ask you: does the Doctor ever mention his shoemaking days to Lucie?"

raw: “Never.”
en: "Never."

raw: “And yet keeps that bench and those tools beside him?”
en: "Yet he keeps the bench and tools next to his bed?"

raw: “Ah!” returned Miss Pross, shaking her head. “But I don’t say he don’t refer to it within himself.”
en: "Yes," said Miss Pross, shaking her head. "But that doesn't mean he doesn't think about it."

raw: “Do you believe that he thinks of it much?”
en: "Do you believe he thinks of it often?"

raw: “I do,” said Miss Pross.
en: "I do," said Miss Pross.

raw: “Do you imagine--” Mr.
en: "Do you imagine, " Mr.

raw: Lorry had begun, when Miss Pross took him up short with:
en: Lorry began to say, before Miss Pross cut him off abruptly:

raw: “Never imagine anything.
en: "Never imagine anything," Miss Pross interrupted.

raw: Have no imagination at all.”
en: "Don't use your imagination."

raw: “I stand corrected; do you suppose--you go so far as to suppose, sometimes?”
en: "I stand corrected. Do you suppose, then?"

raw: “Now and then,” said Miss Pross.
en: "Now and then," she admitted.

raw: “Do you suppose,” Mr.
en: "Do you suppose," Mr.

raw: Lorry went on, with a laughing twinkle in his bright eye, as it looked kindly at her, “that Doctor Manette has any theory of his own, preserved through all those years, relative to the cause of his being so oppressed; perhaps, even to the name of his oppressor?”
en: Lorry asked with a twinkle in his eye, "that Doctor Manette has his own theory about why he was imprisoned, or knows the name of the person who put him there?"

raw: “I don’t suppose anything about it but what Ladybird tells me.”
en: "I only know what Ladybird tells me."

raw: “And that is--?”
en: "And what is that?"

raw: “That she thinks he has.”
en: "She thinks he does."

raw: “Now don’t be angry at my asking all these questions; because I am a mere dull man of business, and you are a woman of business.”
en: "Please don't be angry with my questions. I am just a dull businessman, and you are a practical woman."

raw: “Dull?” Miss Pross inquired, with placidity.
en: "Dull?" Miss Pross asked calmly.

raw: Rather wishing his modest adjective away, Mr.
en: Wishing he hadn't used that word, Mr.

raw: Lorry replied, “No, no, no.
en: Lorry quickly said, "No, no.

raw: Surely not. To return to business:--Is it not remarkable that Doctor Manette, unquestionably innocent of any crime as we are all well assured he is, should never touch upon that question?
en: But to return to the subject: isn't it strange that the Doctor, who is clearly innocent, never speaks of his imprisonment?

raw: I will not say with me, though he had business relations with me many years ago, and we are now intimate; I will say with the fair daughter to whom he is so devotedly attached, and who is so devotedly attached to him?
en: I won't just say with me, even though we had business ties years ago and are now close friends; I will say with his beautiful daughter, whom he loves so deeply and who loves him just as much?"

raw: Believe me, Miss Pross, I don’t approach the topic with you, out of curiosity, but out of zealous interest.”
en: "Believe me, Miss Pross, I am not bringing this up out of mere curiosity, but out of genuine, deep care for him."

raw: “Well! To the best of my understanding, and bad’s the best, you’ll tell me,” said Miss Pross, softened by the tone of the apology, “he is afraid of the whole subject.”
en: "Well," said Miss Pross, softened by his apology, "I think he is simply terrified of the whole subject."

raw: “Afraid?”
en: "Terrified?"

raw: “It’s plain enough, I should think, why he may be.
en: "I should think it's obvious enough why he might be.

raw: It’s a dreadful remembrance.
en: It is a horrible memory.

raw: Besides that, his loss of himself grew out of it.
en: Besides, he lost his mind because of it.

raw: Not knowing how he lost himself, or how he recovered himself, he may never feel certain of not losing himself again.
en: Since he doesn't know exactly how he lost his mind or how he recovered, he might fear losing it again.

raw: That alone wouldn’t make the subject pleasant, I should think.”
en: That would make anyone avoid the subject."

raw: It was a profounder remark than Mr.
en: This was a deeper observation than Mr.

raw: Lorry had looked for. “True,” said he, “and fearful to reflect upon.
en: Lorry had expected. "True," he replied, "and it is frightening to think about.

raw: Yet, a doubt lurks in my mind, Miss Pross, whether it is good for Doctor Manette to have that suppression always shut up within him.
en: Still, I have a lingering doubt, Miss Pross, about whether it's good for Doctor Manette to keep all of those feelings bottled up inside him.

raw: Indeed, it is this doubt and the uneasiness it sometimes causes me that has led me to our present confidence.”
en: Yet I worry if keeping it bottled up inside is good for him."

raw: “Can’t be helped,” said Miss Pross, shaking her head. “Touch that string, and he instantly changes for the worse.
en: "It can't be helped," Miss Pross said, shaking her head. "If you bring that up, he instantly changes for the worse.

raw: Better leave it alone.
en: "If we bring it up, he immediately gets worse.

raw: In short, must leave it alone, like or no like.
en: It is best to leave it alone.

raw: Sometimes, he gets up in the dead of the night, and will be heard, by us overhead there, walking up and down, walking up and down, in his room.
en: Sometimes he gets up in the middle of the night and walks up and down his room for hours.

raw: Ladybird has learnt to know then that his mind is walking up and down, walking up and down, in his old prison.
en: Ladybird knows this means his mind is pacing in his old prison cell.

raw: She hurries to him, and they go on together, walking up and down, walking up and down, until he is composed.
en: She goes to him, and they walk up and down together in silence until he calms down.

raw: But he never says a word of the true reason of his restlessness, to her, and she finds it best not to hint at it to him.
en: But he never says a word to her about the real reason for his restlessness, and she finds it's best not to even hint at it with him.

raw: In silence they go walking up and down together, walking up and down together, till her love and company have brought him to himself.”
en: They just walk together until her presence brings him back to himself."

raw: Notwithstanding Miss Pross’s denial of her own imagination, there was a perception of the pain of being monotonously haunted by one sad idea, in her repetition of the phrase, walking up and down, which testified to her possessing such a thing.
en: Even though Miss Pross claimed she had no imagination, the way she kept repeating the phrase 'walking up and down' showed she understood the pain of being endlessly haunted by one sad thought.

raw: The corner has been mentioned as a wonderful corner for echoes; it had begun to echo so resoundingly to the tread of coming feet, that it seemed as though the very mention of that weary pacing to and fro had set it going.
en: That corner was famous for its echoes, and it began to echo so loudly with the sound of approaching footsteps that it felt as if just mentioning the doctor's endless pacing had triggered it.

raw: “Here they are!” said Miss Pross, rising to break up the conference; “and now we shall have hundreds of people pretty soon!”
en: "Here they are!" said Miss Pross, standing up. "And now we will have hundreds of people!"

raw: It was such a curious corner in its acoustical properties, such a peculiar Ear of a place, that as Mr.
en: The corner had such strange acoustics and picked up sounds so well, like a giant ear, that as Mr.

raw: Lorry stood at the open window, looking for the father and daughter whose steps he heard, he fancied they would never approach.
en: Lorry felt as he looked out the window that the footsteps would never arrive.

raw: Not only would the echoes die away, as though the steps had gone; but, echoes of other steps that never came would be heard in their stead, and would die away for good when they seemed close at hand.
en: Not only would the echoes fade away as if the footsteps had passed, but echoes of other footsteps that never actually arrived would take their place, only to fade away just as they sounded close.

raw: However, father and daughter did at last appear, and Miss Pross was ready at the street door to receive them.
en: Finally, the father and daughter appeared, and Miss Pross went to open the door.

raw: Miss Pross was a pleasant sight, albeit wild, and red, and grim, taking off her darling’s bonnet when she came up-stairs, and touching it up with the ends of her handkerchief, and blowing the dust off it, and folding her mantle ready for laying by, and smoothing her rich hair with as much pride as she could possibly have taken in her own hair if she had been the vainest and handsomest of women.
en: Miss Pross was a pleasant sight, even if she looked a bit wild, red-faced, and grim. She took off her darling's bonnet when she came upstairs, dusted it with her handkerchief, folded her cloak, and smoothed her rich hair with as much pride as if she were the most vain and beautiful woman tending to her own hair.

raw: Her darling was a pleasant sight too, embracing her and thanking her, and protesting against her taking so much trouble for her--which last she only dared to do playfully, or Miss Pross, sorely hurt, would have retired to her own chamber and cried.
en: Lucie was also a pleasant sight, hugging Miss Pross and thanking her for her trouble, which she had to do playfully, or Miss Pross would get upset and cry in her room.

raw: The Doctor was a pleasant sight too, looking on at them, and telling Miss Pross how she spoilt Lucie, in accents and with eyes that had as much spoiling in them as Miss Pross had, and would have had more if it were possible.
en: The Doctor was a pleasant sight too, watching them and telling Miss Pross how she spoiled Lucie, though his own voice and eyes showed just as much spoiling as Miss Pross did, if not more.

raw: Mr.
en: Mr.

raw: Lorry was a pleasant sight too, beaming at all this in his little wig, and thanking his bachelor stars for having lighted him in his declining years to a Home. But, no Hundreds of people came to see the sights, and Mr.
en: Lorry was also a pleasant sight, smiling at all this in his little wig and thanking his lucky stars for guiding him to a real home in his older years. But no hundreds of people came to see these sights, and Mr.

raw: Lorry looked in vain for the fulfilment of Miss Pross’s prediction.
en: But no "hundreds of people" arrived.

raw: Dinner-time, and still no Hundreds of people.
en: By dinner time, there was still no crowd.

raw: In the arrangements of the little household, Miss Pross took charge of the lower regions, and always acquitted herself marvellously.
en: In managing the little household, Miss Pross took charge of the kitchen and downstairs areas, and she always did a marvelous job.

raw: Her dinners, of a very modest quality, were so well cooked and so well served, and so neat in their contrivances, half English and half French, that nothing could be better.
en: Her modest dinners were so perfectly cooked, well-served, and cleverly prepared—half English and half French—that nothing could be better.

raw: Miss Pross’s friendship being of the thoroughly practical kind, she had ravaged Soho and the adjacent provinces, in search of impoverished French, who, tempted by shillings and half-crowns, would impart culinary mysteries to her.
en: In her practical way, she had searched Soho for poor French immigrants who, for a few shillings, taught her their cooking secrets.

raw: From these decayed sons and daughters of Gaul, she had acquired such wonderful arts, that the woman and girl who formed the staff of domestics regarded her as quite a Sorceress, or Cinderella’s Godmother: who would send out for a fowl, a rabbit, a vegetable or two from the garden, and change them into anything she pleased.
en: From these poor French exiles, she had learned such wonderful cooking skills that the maids saw her as a sorceress or Cinderella's Fairy Godmother. She could take a simple chicken, a rabbit, or some vegetables and magically turn them into whatever delicious dish she wanted.

raw: On Sundays, Miss Pross dined at the Doctor’s table, but on other days persisted in taking her meals at unknown periods, either in the lower regions, or in her own room on the second floor--a blue chamber, to which no one but her Ladybird ever gained admittance.
en: On Sundays, Miss Pross ate with the family, though on other days she ate alone in the kitchen or in her private blue room upstairs.

raw: On this occasion, Miss Pross, responding to Ladybird’s pleasant face and pleasant efforts to please her, unbent exceedingly; so the dinner was very pleasant, too.
en: Today, she was in a very good mood, and the dinner was very pleasant.

raw: It was an oppressive day, and, after dinner, Lucie proposed that the wine should be carried out under the plane-tree, and they should sit there in the air. As everything turned upon her, and revolved about her, they went out under the plane-tree, and she carried the wine down for the special benefit of Mr.
en: It was a hot, stuffy day, and after dinner, Lucie suggested they take the wine outside and sit in the fresh air under the plane tree. Since everyone adored her and did whatever she asked, they went out under the tree, and she brought the wine down especially for Mr.

raw: Lorry.
en: They went out, and Lucie poured Mr.

raw: She had installed herself, some time before, as Mr.
en: She had taken it upon herself, a while ago, to act as Mr.

raw: Lorry’s cup-bearer; and while they sat under the plane-tree, talking, she kept his glass replenished. Mysterious backs and ends of houses peeped at them as they talked, and the plane-tree whispered to them in its own way above their heads.
en: Lorry's personal wine-pourer. While they sat under the tree talking, she kept his glass full. The mysterious backs of nearby houses seemed to peek at them, and the leaves of the plane tree whispered above their heads.

raw: Still, the Hundreds of people did not present themselves. Mr.
en: Still, the expected crowd did not show up.

raw: Darnay presented himself while they were sitting under the plane-tree, but he was only One.
en: Charles Darnay arrived, but he was only one person.

raw: Doctor Manette received him kindly, and so did Lucie.
en: Doctor Manette and Lucie received him warmly.

raw: But, Miss Pross suddenly became afflicted with a twitching in the head and body, and retired into the house. She was not unfrequently the victim of this disorder, and she called it, in familiar conversation, “a fit of the jerks.”
en: But suddenly, Miss Pross started twitching all over and hurried back into the house. She suffered from this fairly often, casually calling it 'a fit of the jerks.'

raw: The Doctor was in his best condition, and looked specially young.
en: The Doctor was in high spirits and looked remarkably young.

raw: The resemblance between him and Lucie was very strong at such times, and as they sat side by side, she leaning on his shoulder, and he resting his arm on the back of her chair, it was very agreeable to trace the likeness.
en: The resemblance between him and Lucie was very strong in moments like this, and as they sat together—with her leaning on his shoulder and his arm resting on her chair—it was lovely to see how much they looked alike.

raw: He had been talking all day, on many subjects, and with unusual vivacity. “Pray, Doctor Manette,” said Mr. Darnay, as they sat under the plane-tree--and he said it in the natural pursuit of the topic in hand, which happened to be the old buildings of London--“have you seen much of the Tower?”
en: He had been talking all day about many subjects with unusual energy. "Tell me, Doctor Manette," Mr. Darnay asked as they sat under the tree, casually continuing their conversation about old London buildings, "have you seen much of the Tower of London?"

raw: “Lucie and I have been there; but only casually.
en: "Lucie and I have been there, but only briefly.

raw: We have seen enough of it, to know that it teems with interest; little more.”
en: We know it is very interesting, but not much more."

raw: “_I_ have been there, as you remember,” said Darnay, with a smile, though reddening a little angrily, “in another character, and not in a character that gives facilities for seeing much of it.
en: "I was kept there, as you remember," Darnay said with a slight smile, though he colored slightly.

raw: They told me a curious thing when I was there.”
en: "They told me a strange story when I was there."

raw: “What was that?” Lucie asked.
en: "What was that?" Lucie asked.

raw: “In making some alterations, the workmen came upon an old dungeon, which had been, for many years, built up and forgotten.
en: "While making some changes, the workmen discovered an old dungeon that had been walled up and completely forgotten for many years.

raw: Every stone of its inner wall was covered by inscriptions which had been carved by prisoners--dates, names, complaints, and prayers.
en: Every stone on the inside walls was covered with carvings made by prisoners, including dates, names, complaints, and prayers.

raw: Upon a corner stone in an angle of the wall, one prisoner, who seemed to have gone to execution, had cut as his last work, three letters.
en: In a corner stone, one prisoner who was executed had hurriedly carved three letters.

raw: They were done with some very poor instrument, and hurriedly, with an unsteady hand.
en: They were carved in a hurry with a very poor tool and a shaky hand.

raw: At first, they were read as D.
en: I.

raw: I. C.; but, on being more carefully examined, the last letter was found to be G.
en: C., but on closer inspection, the last letter was a G.

raw: There was no record or legend of any prisoner with those initials, and many fruitless guesses were made what the name could have been.
en: There was no record of a prisoner with those initials, and people guessed what it meant.

raw: At length, it was suggested that the letters were not initials, but the complete word, DIG.
en: Finally, someone suggested the letters spelled the word 'DIG'.

raw: The floor was examined very carefully under the inscription, and, in the earth beneath a stone, or tile, or some fragment of paving, were found the ashes of a paper, mingled with the ashes of a small leathern case or bag.
en: The floor beneath the writing was examined very carefully, and under a loose paving stone, they found the ashes of a piece of paper mixed with the ashes of a small leather bag.

raw: What the unknown prisoner had written will never be read, but he had written something, and hidden it away to keep it from the gaoler.”
en: What the prisoner wrote will never be known, but he had hidden it from his guards."

raw: “My father,” exclaimed Lucie, “you are ill!”
en: "Father!" Lucie cried. "You look ill!"

raw: He had suddenly started up, with his hand to his head. His manner and his look quite terrified them all.
en: The Doctor had suddenly stood up, putting his hand to his head with a terrified look.

raw: “No, my dear, not ill.
en: "No, my dear, not ill.

raw: There are large drops of rain falling, and they made me start.
en: A few large rain drops fell on me and startled me.

raw: We had better go in.”
en: We should go inside."

raw: He recovered himself almost instantly.
en: He recovered his composure almost immediately.

raw: Rain was really falling in large drops, and he showed the back of his hand with rain-drops on it.
en: Rain was indeed starting to fall, and he showed them the drops on his hand.

raw: But, he said not a single word in reference to the discovery that had been told of, and, as they went into the house, the business eye of Mr.
en: But he said nothing about the story Darnay had told. As they went inside, Mr.

raw: Lorry either detected, or fancied it detected, on his face, as it turned towards Charles Darnay, the same singular look that had been upon it when it turned towards him in the passages of the Court House.
en: Lorry noticed the same strange look on the Doctor's face as he looked at Darnay, the same expression he had seen at the courthouse.

raw: He recovered himself so quickly, however, that Mr.
en: He recovered so quickly, however, that Mr.

raw: Lorry had doubts of his business eye.
en: Lorry doubted what he had seen.

raw: The arm of the golden giant in the hall was not more steady than he was, when he stopped under it to remark to them that he was not yet proof against slight surprises (if he ever would be), and that the rain had startled him.
en: He was as steady as a statue when he stopped to tell them that he still got startled easily, and that the sudden rain had simply caught him off guard.

raw: Tea-time, and Miss Pross making tea, with another fit of the jerks upon her, and yet no Hundreds of people.
en: At tea time, Miss Pross served tea, still twitching, but there was still no crowd.

raw: Mr. Carton had lounged in, but he made only Two.
en: Sydney Carton arrived, making the guests only two.

raw: The night was so very sultry, that although they sat with doors and windows open, they were overpowered by heat. When the tea-table was done with, they all moved to one of the windows, and looked out into the heavy twilight.
en: The night was so muggy that, even with the doors and windows open, the heat was overwhelming. After tea, they all moved to one of the windows and looked out into the heavy twilight.

raw: Lucie sat by her father; Darnay sat beside her; Carton leaned against a window. The curtains were long and white, and some of the thunder-gusts that whirled into the corner, caught them up to the ceiling, and waved them like spectral wings.
en: Lucie sat next to her father, Darnay sat beside her, and Carton leaned against a window. The long white curtains were caught by gusts of wind from the storm, whipping up to the ceiling and waving around like ghostly wings.

raw: “The rain-drops are still falling, large, heavy, and few,” said Doctor Manette. “It comes slowly.”
en: "The rain drops are still few and heavy," said Doctor Manette. "The storm is coming slowly."

raw: “It comes surely,” said Carton.
en: "It is coming surely," said Carton.

raw: They spoke low, as people watching and waiting mostly do; as people in a dark room, watching and waiting for Lightning, always do.
en: They spoke quietly, the way people do when waiting for lightning in a dark room.

raw: There was a great hurry in the streets of people speeding away to get shelter before the storm broke; the wonderful corner for echoes resounded with the echoes of footsteps coming and going, yet not a footstep was there.
en: The streets below were busy with people running for shelter. The quiet corner echoed with the sound of footsteps, though no one was there.

raw: “A multitude of people, and yet a solitude!” said Darnay, when they had listened for a while.
en: "A crowd of footsteps, yet the street is empty!" Darnay remarked.

raw: “Is it not impressive, Mr.
en: "Isn't it strange, Mr.

raw: Darnay?” asked Lucie. “Sometimes, I have sat here of an evening, until I have fancied--but even the shade of a foolish fancy makes me shudder to-night, when all is so black and solemn--”
en: Darnay?" Lucie asked. "Sometimes I sit here in the evening and imagine, though the fancy frightens me tonight in the dark, "

raw: “Let us shudder too.
en: "Tell us.

raw: We may know what it is.”
en: We want to know."

raw: “It will seem nothing to you.
en: "It sounds silly.

raw: Such whims are only impressive as we originate them, I think; they are not to be communicated. I have sometimes sat alone here of an evening, listening, until I have made the echoes out to be the echoes of all the footsteps that are coming by-and-bye into our lives.”
en: I have sat here alone, listening to the echoes, until I imagined they were the footsteps of all the people who will enter our lives in the future."

raw: “There is a great crowd coming one day into our lives, if that be so,”  Sydney Carton struck in, in his moody way.
en: "There is a huge crowd coming into our lives, then," Sydney Carton remarked gloomily.

raw: The footsteps were incessant, and the hurry of them became more and more rapid.
en: The echoes of footsteps grew faster and louder as the storm approached.

raw: The corner echoed and re-echoed with the tread of feet; some, as it seemed, under the windows; some, as it seemed, in the room; some coming, some going, some breaking off, some stopping altogether; all in the distant streets, and not one within sight.
en: The corner echoed loudly with the sound of footsteps. Some sounded like they were right under the windows, and others seemed to be inside the room. There were footsteps coming, going, and stopping suddenly, yet they were all actually out in the distant streets, with no one anywhere in sight.

raw: “Are all these footsteps destined to come to all of us, Miss Manette, or are we to divide them among us?”
en: "Are all these people coming to all of us, Miss Manette, or will we divide them?"

raw: “I don’t know, Mr.
en: "I don't know, Mr.

raw: Darnay; I told you it was a foolish fancy, but you asked for it.
en: Darnay. It was just a foolish fancy.

raw: When I have yielded myself to it, I have been alone, and then I have imagined them the footsteps of the people who are to come into my life, and my father’s.”
en: When I let myself get lost in the sound, usually when I'm alone, I imagine they are the footsteps of the people who will eventually walk into my life and my father's life."

raw: “I take them into mine!” said Carton. “_I_ ask no questions and make no stipulations.
en: "I will take them into mine!" said Carton. "I make no conditions.

raw: There is a great crowd bearing down upon us, Miss Manette, and I see them--by the Lightning.” He added the last words, after there had been a vivid flash which had shown him lounging in the window.
en: A huge crowd is coming toward us, Miss Manette, and I see them, by the lightning." He spoke as a bright flash illuminated his figure by the window.

raw: “And I hear them!” he added again, after a peal of thunder. “Here they come, fast, fierce, and furious!”
en: "And I hear them!" he added after a clap of thunder. "Here they come, fast and fierce!"

raw: It was the rush and roar of rain that he typified, and it stopped him, for no voice could be heard in it.
en: He was referring to the sudden downpour of rain, which drowned out his voice.

raw: A memorable storm of thunder and lightning broke with that sweep of water, and there was not a moment’s interval in crash, and fire, and rain, until after the moon rose at midnight.
en: A powerful storm of thunder, lightning, and rain raged until midnight when the moon finally came out.

raw: The great bell of Saint Paul’s was striking one in the cleared air, when Mr.
en: The great bell of Saint Paul's Cathedral was striking one o'clock in the clear night air, when Mr.

raw: Lorry, escorted by Jerry, high-booted and bearing a lantern, set forth on his return-passage to Clerkenwell.
en: Paul's Cathedral was striking one in the clear night air when Mr.

raw: There were solitary patches of road on the way between Soho and Clerkenwell, and Mr.
en: Lorry, escorted by Jerry carrying a lantern, set out for home.

raw: Lorry, mindful of foot-pads, always retained Jerry for this service: though it was usually performed a good two hours earlier.
en: Because some stretches of the road were dark and dangerous, Mr. Lorry always had Jerry walk with him.

raw: “What a night it has been!
en: "What a storm!

raw: Almost a night, Jerry,” said Mr.
en: It was enough to wake the dead, Jerry," Mr.

raw: Lorry, “to bring the dead out of their graves.”
en: Lorry, "it's enough to wake the dead from their graves."

raw: “I never see the night myself, master--nor yet I don’t expect to--what would do that,” answered Jerry.
en: "I've never seen a night that could do that, master," Jerry replied.

raw: “Good night, Mr.
en: "Good night, Mr.

raw: Carton,” said the man of business. “Good night, Mr.
en: Carton. Good night, Mr. Darnay," Mr.

raw: Darnay.
en: Lorry called out.

raw: Shall we ever see such a night again, together!”
en: "Will we ever see such a night together again?"

raw: Perhaps.
en: Perhaps.

raw: Perhaps, see the great crowd of people with its rush and roar, bearing down upon them, too.
en: And perhaps they would see that great crowd of people, with its rush and roar, coming down upon them as well.
